lesson_title: The Pea That Owns the Stadium
hook_text: You, your phone, this planet — almost entirely EMPTY SPACE. Here's how we found out.
clip_script: Put an atom on the centre spot of a big soccer stadium and inflate it until the atom fills the whole ground. The nucleus — the part holding all the protons and neutrons — is a single pea on the kickoff dot. Everything else, out to the highest row of seats, is the electrons' territory: almost completely empty space, patrolled by particles so light no scale bothers with them. That pea owns essentially ALL the mass of the atom, and all the positive charge — while the stands hold the matching negatives, one electron for every proton. And how do we know the pea is really there? Scientists fired tiny, fast particles at gold foil thinner than a page, expecting them all to punch through soft, spread-out atoms. Nearly all did — an empty stadium. But roughly one in several thousand slammed into something and bounced back hard. You only bounce off a pea if there IS a pea: tiny, dense, charged. That bounce is how humanity discovered the nucleus. Everything you will ever touch is stadiums of emptiness around stubborn little peas — held together by nothing but the attraction between plus and minus. Chemistry is what the crowd in the stands gets up to.
visual_style: A floodlit stadium at night morphing into an atom — a glowing pea at the centre spot, faint electron sparks circling the stands; alpha particles streak through as comets, one ricocheting violently back toward the camera.
mood: Awe-first physics — the emptiness of matter made cinematic.
pacing: Slow inflating zoom, quiet emptiness beat, sudden ricochet jolt, reflective closing line.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and own the atom from pea to top floor.
